Literal

/LIT-er-uhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Literal means taking words in their basic, most obvious sense, without exaggeration or metaphor.

When Maya groaned that she had a mountain of homework, her little brother took her words in a literal sense and asked where the mountain was.

Worked Example

The translator warned that a literal version of the poem would keep every word but lose the joke hidden inside it.

A literal version sticks to the plain, exact sense of each word. Because jokes often live in wordplay and figurative meaning, the most exact translation can be the least faithful to the poem's spirit.

How Literal Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

exact

exact: precisely accurate, keeping to the stated sense

word-for-word

word-for-word: following the original wording exactly

plain

plain: sticking to the obvious, unadorned meaning

Antonyms

figurative

figurative: using words in imaginative, non-literal ways

metaphorical

metaphorical: describing one thing in terms of another

How Strong Is It? — plain → literal → verbatim

plain vs. literal

plain vs. literal: A plain statement avoids fancy language; a literal reading goes further, refusing any meaning beyond the exact words.

verbatim vs. literal

verbatim vs. literal: A literal translation keeps each word's plain sense; a verbatim transcript repeats the exact words themselves, one by one.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — liter-

Root — liter-: letter - from Latin littera

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to - Latin adjective-forming -alis

Put it together

Put it together: 'Relating to the letters' - a literal meaning is the one you get by taking the letters and words exactly as written, with nothing added and nothing imagined.

Use the root in a new word: literacy

Word Choice

Neutral; everyday and academic use

Literal means sticking to the plain, exact sense of the words - a literal translation, a literal reading, taking a phrase literally. It contrasts with figurative language such as metaphor and idiom. Watch for the casual misuse of 'literally' as a mere intensifier ('I literally died'); in careful writing and on the SAT, literal always signals the exact, non-figurative meaning - not a vague 'actual' or 'real.'
